# SQL Faker — fake user data generated by PostgreSQL stored procedures

SQL Faker is a small "Faker" library written entirely in **PL/pgSQL / SQL** (PostgreSQL 14+).
Every fake value — names, addresses, coordinates, phone numbers, e-mails, physical
attributes and Markov-chain text — is produced inside the database. The web application
only calls `fk_users(...)` and renders the rows.

```sql
SELECT full_name, address, phone, email
FROM fk_users('de_DE', 42, 0);          -- locale, seed, batch index (10 users per batch)
```

| full_name | address | phone | email |
|---|---|---|---|
| Volker Krämer | Neustieg 1, 16404 Berlin | +49 152 42420636 | volker_kraemer@arcor.de |
| Herr Dr. Anton Brenner | Mittelgasse 39, 42729 Solingen, Nordrhein-Westfalen | 0709 8288275 | antonbrenner@web.de |
| … | … | … | … |

## 1. Quick start

```bash
createdb faker
scripts/init_db.sh faker                 # loads db/*.sql in order
psql -d faker -c "SELECT * FROM fk_users('en_US', 2024, 0)"
psql -d faker -c "SELECT * FROM fk_benchmark('en_US', 10000)"
```

Files in `db/` (loaded in this order):

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `01_schema.sql` | tables |
| `02_random.sql` | deterministic random primitives (`fk_random*`) |
| `03_lookup.sql` | data loading, weighted picking, templating, Markov chain builder |
| `10_data_en_US.sql`, `11_data_de_DE.sql` | locale data (one file per locale) |
| `20_generators.sql` | field generators and the public API (`fk_user`, `fk_users`, `fk_benchmark`) |
| `90_finalize.sql` | `CALL fk_reindex()` + build Markov chains |

## 2. Architecture

The library is split into small layers. Each layer only uses the layers below it.

```
 ┌──────────────────────────── public API ─────────────────────────────┐
 │ fk_users(locale, seed, batch, size)  fk_user(...)  fk_benchmark(...)│
 ├──────────────────────────── field generators ───────────────────────┤
 │ fk_gender  fk_full_name  fk_address  fk_geolocation  fk_phone        │
 │ fk_email   fk_physical   fk_markov_text                              │
 ├──────────────────────────── lookup & formatting ────────────────────┤
 │ fk_pick  fk_pick_city  fk_render  fk_transliterate  fk_random_digits │
 ├──────────────────────────── random primitives ──────────────────────┤
 │ fk_random  fk_random_int  fk_random_bool  fk_random_normal           │
 │ fk_random_normal_clamped  fk_random_sphere  fk_record_key            │
 ├──────────────────────────── data (per locale rows) ─────────────────┤
 │ locales  words  cities  distributions  text_corpus → markov_chain    │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 2.1 Reproducibility model

There is **no RNG state** anywhere. Every random number is a pure function

```
U = fk_random(key, stream)        -- uniform in [0, 1)
key    = '<locale>:<seed>:<position>' || ':<field>'     e.g. 'de_DE:42:17:addr'
stream = small integer numbering draws inside the field (0, 1, 2 …)
```

* `position = batch_index * batch_size + index_in_batch`, so user #17 of seed 42 is
  the same whether you load it as batch 1 / index 7 or as part of a batch of 100.
* Identical `(locale, seed, position)` always gives the identical user, on any
  server, in any order, without generating the previous users first.
* Each field has its own key suffix (`:name`, `:addr`, `:geo`, `:phone`, `:mail`,
  `:body`, `:text`, `:gender`), so fields are independent and editing one generator
  never changes the values of another field.
* Different locales use different keys, so the same seed gives unrelated people in
  different regions.

This is a *counter-based* RNG (like Philox / SplitMix used as a hash). It lets
PostgreSQL generate any batch directly and in parallel.

### 2.2 Data model (extensible by design)

No table is locale-specific; every row carries a `locale` column. **A new locale is
added by inserting rows only** (see [§6](#6-adding-a-new-locale)).

| Table | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `locales(code, name, units)` | supported regions; `units` = `metric` / `imperial` controls how height/weight are printed |
| `words(locale, category, value, weight, ord, cum_hi)` | **all vocabulary and all format templates**, weighted. `ord` / `cum_hi` are maintained by `fk_reindex()` |
| `cities(locale, city, region, region_code, postal, weight, cum_hi)` | cities with state / Bundesland and postal-code pattern |
| `distributions(locale, attribute, gender, mean, sd, min_value, max_value)` | parameters of normal distributions (`height_cm`, `bmi`, `age`) |
| `category_sizes(locale, category, n, total_weight)` | cache of category sizes, filled by `fk_reindex()` |
| `text_corpus(locale, body)` | source text for the Markov chain |
| `markov_chain(locale, word, successors[])` | first-order word chain, built by `fk_build_markov()` |

Categories of `words` used by the generators:

| Category | Used by | en_US example | de_DE example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `first_name_M`, `first_name_F` | name, middle name | James, Mary | Jürgen, Bärbel |
| `last_name` | name, double surname | O'Brien | Müller |
| `title_M`, `title_F` | `{title}` | Mr., Dr. | Herr, Frau |
| `academic` | `{acad}` | — | Dr., Prof. Dr., Dipl.-Ing. |
| `suffix_M`, `suffix_F` | `{suffix}` | Jr., III, PhD | — |
| `fmt_name` | name layout | `{first} {mi}. {last}` | `{first}-{middle} {last}` |
| `street_name`, `street_suffix` | address | Oak + Avenue | Linden + straße |
| `street_dir`, `unit` | address | NE, `Apt. @#` | — |
| `street_adj`, `street_type`, `street_full`, `house_letter` | address | — | Berliner + Straße, Am Markt, 12**a** |
| `house_number` | address (digit pattern) | `@##` | `@#` |
| `fmt_address` | address layout | `{number} {dir} {street} {suffix}, {unit}, {city}, {state_code} {zip}` | `{street}{suffix} {number}, {zip} {city}` |
| `fmt_phone` | phone (digit pattern) | `(%##) %##-####` | `+49 (0)%## ######` |
| `fmt_email`, `email_domain` | e-mail | `{f}{last}{nn}`, gmail.com | `{first}.{last}`, web.de |
| `eye_color`, `hair_color`, `blood_type` | physical | Hazel, Auburn, O+ | Blau, Dunkelblond, A+ |

Data volume (per locale): ~200 male + ~200 female first names, 380–580 last names,
~200 street names, 130–150 cities, 7–14 layouts per field. That gives
> 240 000 first/last combinations per locale before layouts, middle names, titles and
double surnames are applied. Measured over **100 000 users** (seed 123):

| locale | distinct full names | distinct e-mails | distinct addresses | distinct phones |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| en_US | 95 065 | 98 249 | 100 000 | 100 000 |
| de_DE | 89 809 | 98 104 | 100 000 | 99 999 |

## 3. API reference — public procedures

### `fk_users(p_locale text, p_seed bigint, p_batch int, p_batch_size int DEFAULT 10) → TABLE`

Generates one batch of fake users. **This is the only procedure the web app calls.**

| Argument | Description |
|---|---|
| `p_locale` | locale code from `locales` (`'en_US'`, `'de_DE'`). Unknown codes raise `invalid_parameter_value`. |
| `p_seed` | any 64-bit integer chosen by the user |
| `p_batch` | 0-based batch index (`0` = first page, `1` = "next batch", …) |
| `p_batch_size` | users per batch, 1..10000 |

Returned columns:

| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `batch_index`, `index_in_batch` | int | where the row is in the requested batch |
| `position` | bigint | absolute position `batch * size + index` (the value that drives randomness) |
| `gender` | char(1) | `M` / `F` (50/50) |
| `full_name` | text | formatted name incl. optional title / middle name / suffix |
| `first_name`, `last_name` | text | plain parts (used for the e-mail) |
| `address` | text | formatted address |
| `city`, `region`, `postal_code` | text | parts of the address |
| `latitude`, `longitude` | numeric(…,6) | uniform on the sphere |
| `phone`, `email` | text | formatted |
| `age` | int | normal, clamped |
| `height_cm`, `weight_kg` | numeric | normal (height, BMI) |
| `eye_color`, `hair_color`, `blood_type` | text | weighted discrete |
| `physical` | text | height / weight printed in locale units (`5′10″, 165 lb` / `178 cm, 75 kg`) |
| `bio` | text | 1–2 sentences of Markov-chain text in the locale's language |

```sql
SELECT * FROM fk_users('en_US', 7, 0);          -- users 0..9
SELECT * FROM fk_users('en_US', 7, 1);          -- users 10..19 ("next batch")
SELECT * FROM fk_users('en_US', 7, 0, 20);      -- users 0..19 — same people as the two calls above
```

### `fk_user(p_locale text, p_seed bigint, p_position bigint) → record`

One user at an absolute position. Same columns as `fk_users` without the batch columns.
Use it with `generate_series` for arbitrary ranges:

```sql
SELECT u.* FROM generate_series(1000000, 1000004) p, fk_user('de_DE', 1, p) u;
```

### `fk_benchmark(p_locale text, p_count int DEFAULT 10000, p_seed bigint DEFAULT 1) → (locale, users, seconds, users_per_second)`

Generates `p_count` complete users (all columns, including the Markov text) and reports
the speed measured with `clock_timestamp()`.

## 4. API reference — building blocks

Everything below can be used on its own, e.g. to build other generators.

### 4.1 Random primitives (`02_random.sql`)

#### `fk_random(p_key text, p_stream int) → float8`  — uniform U ∈ [0, 1)

`hashtextextended(key, stream)` is PostgreSQL's built-in 64-bit Jenkins *lookup3*
hash. Its second argument is a hash seed, which we use as the stream number. The hash
is stable across versions and platforms because hash partitioning depends on it. The
top 53 bits form the mantissa of a double:

```
U = ((h >> 11) & (2^53 − 1)) / 2^53
```

The function is an `IMMUTABLE` single-expression SQL function, so the planner inlines
it: one call costs ≈ 0.3 µs.

#### `fk_random_int(p_key, p_stream, p_lo int, p_hi int) → int`
Uniform integer in `[lo, hi]`: `lo + floor(U · (hi − lo + 1))`.

#### `fk_random_bool(p_key, p_stream, p_prob float8) → boolean`
Bernoulli trial: `U < p`.

#### `fk_random_normal(p_key, p_stream, p_mean, p_sd) → float8`
Normally distributed value, **Box–Muller transform**:

```
U1 = 1 − fk_random(key, stream)            ∈ (0, 1]   (avoids ln 0)
U2 = fk_random(key || '~bm', stream)       ∈ [0, 1)
Z  = sqrt(−2 · ln U1) · cos(2π · U2)        ~ N(0, 1)
X  = mean + sd · Z
```

#### `fk_random_normal_clamped(p_key, p_stream, p_mean, p_sd, p_min, p_max) → float8`
`least(max, greatest(min, normal))`. It cuts off impossible tails (negative height,
age 7) and keeps the bell shape. It is deliberately **not** `STRICT`: a STRICT SQL
function with a non-strict body (`least`/`greatest`) cannot be inlined.

#### `fk_random_sphere(p_key, p_stream) → (latitude float8, longitude float8)`
A point **uniformly distributed on the sphere surface** (constant PDF per unit area).

Taking `lat` uniformly in [−90, 90] would be wrong. The area of a latitude band is
proportional to `cos(lat)`, so uniform latitudes would crowd points at the poles.
By Archimedes' hat-box theorem, the projection `z = sin(lat)` of a uniform point on
the sphere is uniform on [−1, 1]. So:

```
longitude = 360 · U1 − 180                 uniform in [−180, 180)
latitude  = degrees(asin(2 · U2 − 1))      PDF ∝ cos(latitude)
```

Check over 50 000 points: 49.9 % lie in |lat| < 30° (theory: sin 30° = 50 %) and
13.4 % in |lat| > 60° (theory: 1 − sin 60° = 13.4 %). Uniform latitudes would give
33.3 % in both bands.

#### `fk_random_digits(p_pattern text, p_key, p_stream) → text`
Fills a digit pattern character by character (`stream + i` for character i):

| Symbol | Replaced by |
|---|---|
| `#` | 0–9 |
| `@` | 1–9 (no leading zero) |
| `%` | 2–9 (NANP area codes / exchanges) |
| anything else | copied unchanged |

`fk_random_digits('(%##) %##-####', 'k', 1)` → `(951) 469-5310`

#### `fk_record_key(p_locale, p_seed bigint, p_position bigint) → text`
Builds the record key `'<locale>:<seed>:<position>'`.

### 4.2 Lookup & formatting (`03_lookup.sql`)

#### `fk_pick(p_locale, p_category, p_key, p_stream) → text`
**Weighted random pick** from `words`, using inverse-CDF sampling over a discrete
distribution:

1. `r = U · total_weight` (total from `category_sizes`)
2. return the first row with `cum_hi > r`, where `cum_hi` = running sum of weights
   in `id` order. This is one range scan on the index `(locale, category, cum_hi)`.

With all weights = 1 this is a uniform pick. The weights encode realistic
frequencies: `Brown^45|Blue^27|…` for eye colours, or `{first} {last}^50` vs
`{title} {first} {last}^10` for name layouts. Returns `NULL` if the category does not
exist for the locale.

#### `fk_pick_city(p_locale, p_key, p_stream) → cities`
Same algorithm over the `cities` table (big cities have larger weights).

#### `fk_render(p_template text, p_names text[], p_values text[]) → text`
Replaces `{name}` placeholders. `NULL` values become empty strings, and repeated
spaces are squeezed.
```sql
SELECT fk_render('{title} {first} {last}', ARRAY['title','first','last'], ARRAY[NULL,'Ann','Lee']);
-- 'Ann Lee'
```

#### `fk_transliterate(p_text) → text`
Lower case; `ä→ae, ö→oe, ü→ue, ß→ss`; other diacritics stripped; everything outside
`[a-z0-9]` removed (`O'Brien → obrien`, `Müller → mueller`). Used for e-mails.

#### Data maintenance procedures

| Procedure | Description |
|---|---|
| `CALL fk_add_words(locale, category, list)` | bulk insert, `list` = `'a\|b^weight\|c'` (`^weight` optional, default 1), duplicates ignored |
| `CALL fk_add_cities(locale, list)` | rows `'City\|Region\|CODE\|postal pattern[\|weight]'` separated by `;` |
| `CALL fk_reindex()` | recomputes `ord`, `cum_hi` and `category_sizes`. **Run after any change to words/cities.** |
| `CALL fk_build_markov(locale)` | rebuilds `markov_chain` of a locale from `text_corpus` |

### 4.3 Field generators (`20_generators.sql`)

All of them take the record key `p_key` and append their own suffix.

#### `fk_gender(p_key) → 'M' | 'F'`
`fk_random_bool(key || ':gender', 0, 0.5)`.

#### `fk_full_name(p_locale, p_key, p_gender) → (full_name, first_name, last_name)`
How name variation works:

1. Pick a **layout** from `fmt_name` (weighted). Placeholders:
   `{first} {middle} {mi} {last} {last2} {title} {acad} {suffix}`.
2. Pick `first_name_<gender>` and `last_name`.
3. Pick **only the optional parts the layout uses** (checked with `strpos`):
   middle name (re-drawn once if equal to the first name), `mi` = middle initial,
   second surname for double names, gendered title, academic degree, gendered suffix.
4. Render with `fk_render`.

Layouts shipped:

| en_US (weight) | de_DE (weight) |
|---|---|
| `{first} {last}` 50 → *Ryan Cooper* | `{first} {last}` 55 → *Jürgen Weiß* |
| `{first} {mi}. {last}` 15 → *Ryan T. Cooper* | `{first} {middle} {last}` 10 → *Hans Peter Lang* |
| `{first} {middle} {last}` 8 | `{first}-{middle} {last}` 5 → *Anna-Lena Vogt* |
| `{title} {first} {last}` 10 → *Mrs. Ann Lee* | `{title} {first} {last}` 10 → *Frau Ute Kolb* |
| `{title} {first} {mi}. {last}` 5 | `{acad} {first} {last}` 8 → *Prof. Dr. Ida Roth* |
| `{first} {last} {suffix}` 4 → *Brett McGee II* | `{title} {acad} {first} {last}` 4 → *Herr Dr. Anton Brenner* |
| `{first} {last}-{last2}` 2 → *Molly Tran-Vaughn* | `{first} {last}-{last2}` 5 |
| `{last}, {first} {mi}.` 3 → *Torres, Calvin L.* | `{last}, {first}` 2, `{title} {last}` 1 |

To change the variations, edit / reweight rows of category `fmt_name`. No code change
is needed.

#### `fk_address(p_locale, p_key) → (address, city, region, postal_code)`
1. Weighted city → city, region, region code, postal pattern (`'100##'`, `'80###'`).
   The postal code is filled with `fk_random_digits`, so it matches the city's real
   prefix.
2. Layout from `fmt_address`, house number pattern from `house_number`.
3. The layout's parts are picked from the street vocabulary:
   * en_US: `{number} {dir} {street} {suffix}, {unit}` → *4591 E Shore Dr, Fl. 5, Newark, NJ 07153*, or *PO Box 628*.
   * de_DE: compound street names `{street}{suffix}` → *Linden* + *straße*; adjective
     form `{adj} {type}` → *Kölner Straße*; fixed names `{full}` → *An der Kirche*;
     house letters → *77a*; optional `D-` prefix or Bundesland.

#### `fk_geolocation(p_key) → (latitude numeric, longitude numeric)`
`fk_random_sphere`, rounded to 6 decimals (~0.1 m). On purpose, the coordinates are
independent of the address: they are uniform over the whole sphere.

#### `fk_phone(p_locale, p_key) → text`
Weighted layout from `fmt_phone` filled by `fk_random_digits`.
en_US: `(%##) %##-####`, `+1 %## %## ####`, `1-%##-%##-####`, extensions `x###` …;
de_DE: landline `0%### ######`, `(0%##) ######`, `+49 (0)%## ######`, mobile
`015# ########`, `+49 17# #######` …

#### `fk_email(p_locale, p_key, p_first, p_last) → text`
Layout from `fmt_email` with `{first} {last} {f} {l}` (transliterated names / initials),
`{nn}` (2 digits), `{nnn}` (3 digits, no leading zero), `{yy}` (year-like 50…09).
Then `'@'` + weighted `email_domain` → `kevin.sommer@yahoo.de`, `ctorres@comcast.net`.

#### `fk_physical(p_locale, p_key, p_gender) → (age, height_cm, weight_kg, eye_color, hair_color, blood_type, summary)`
* **age**, **height** and **BMI** ~ `fk_random_normal_clamped` with locale + gender
  parameters from `distributions`. For example, en_US male height N(175.4, 7.6),
  de_DE female N(166.1, 6.6).
* **weight** = BMI · height², so weight is realistically correlated with height,
  not independent.
* **eye colour**, **hair colour**, **blood type**: weighted `fk_pick`, with locale
  frequencies (blue eyes are more common in de_DE; blood group A+ vs O+).
* **summary** uses locale units: imperial `5′10″, 165 lb`, metric `178 cm, 75 kg`.

Measured over 5 000 en_US users: male height mean 175.6 / sd 7.7, female 161.4 / 7.0.

#### `fk_markov_text(p_locale, p_key, p_sentences int DEFAULT 2, p_max_words int DEFAULT 25) → text`
Random text in the locale's language from a **first-order word Markov chain** (not
lorem ipsum):

* **Model** (`fk_build_markov`): the corpus is split on whitespace, with punctuation
  kept on the token. For every token, the array `successors` stores *every* following
  token with repetitions, so choosing a uniform array element is choosing proportionally
  to the bigram frequency. After a token ending in `.`, `!` or `?`, the next token is
  stored as a successor of `''` (start of sentence).
* **Walk**: start at `''`; `next = successors[1 + floor(U · n)]`, where U is
  `fk_random(key, step)`; a sentence ends on `. ! ?` or is closed with `.` after
  `p_max_words` words; stop after `p_sentences` sentences.

Examples: *"The water was always told with warm bread and the journey shorter."* /
*"Im Sommer fuhren wir an der Bibliothek und einen Marathon laufen, fünfzig Bücher lesen
und dass es ist einfach."*

## 5. Benchmark

`fk_benchmark` (in-database) and `scripts/benchmark.py` (end-to-end through Python,
1 000-user batches). Both generate **complete** users, including Markov text.
Setup: one PostgreSQL 16 backend (single core), Intel i5-13500H, 100 000 users per locale.

| locale | mode | users | seconds | **users / s** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| de_DE | in-database | 100 000 | 47.8 | **2 093** |
| de_DE | end-to-end | 100 000 | 49.0 | **2 040** |
| en_US | in-database | 100 000 | 49.9 | **2 006** |
| en_US | end-to-end | 100 000 | 50.8 | **1 970** |

≈ **2 000 users / second per core**, i.e. ~0.5 ms per user. A 10-user page takes ~5 ms.

Notes from profiling (`track_functions = all`):
* SQL-language functions that cannot be inlined are **re-planned on every call**
  (≈70 µs). Single-expression primitives are therefore kept inlinable, and procedures
  with real queries/loops are PL/pgSQL, whose plans are cached.
* The Markov walk is a loop with one primary-key lookup per word. A recursive CTE was
  4× slower, because the planner duplicated the lookup sub-plan.

## 6. Adding a new locale

No schema or code changes are needed. Example for `fr_FR`:

```sql
INSERT INTO locales VALUES ('fr_FR', 'Français (France)', 'metric');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'first_name_M', 'Louis|Gabriel|Jules|…');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'first_name_F', 'Camille|Léa|Chloé|…');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'last_name',    'Martin|Bernard|Dubois|…');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'title_M', 'M.');  CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'title_F', 'Mme^70|Mlle^30');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'fmt_name',     '{first} {last}^70|{title} {first} {last}^20|{first}-{middle} {last}^10');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'street_name',  'de la République|Victor Hugo|des Lilas|…');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'street_suffix','rue^60|avenue^20|boulevard^10|place^10');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'house_number', '@^40|@#^50|@##^10');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'fmt_address',  '{number} {suffix} {street}, {zip} {city}');
CALL fk_add_cities('fr_FR', 'Paris|Île-de-France|IDF|750##|5;Lyon|Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes|ARA|6900#|2');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'fmt_phone',    '0@ ## ## ## ##^70|+33 @ ## ## ## ##^30');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'fmt_email',    '{first}.{last}|{f}{last}{nn}');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'email_domain', 'orange.fr^30|gmail.com^30|free.fr^20|laposte.net^20');
CALL fk_add_words('fr_FR', 'eye_color',    'Marron^50|Bleu^25|Vert^15|Noisette^10');
-- … hair_color, blood_type, distributions rows, text_corpus …
CALL fk_reindex();
CALL fk_build_markov('fr_FR');
```

The new locale then appears automatically in the web UI's region selector.

## 7. Web application

`app/app.py` (Flask + psycopg 3) contains no generation logic:

| Route | Description |
|---|---|
| `GET /?locale=&seed=` | page with the first batch; changing region / seed regenerates |
| `GET /batch?locale=&seed=&batch=` | HTML rows of the next batch (infinite scroll / *Next batch*) |
| `GET /api/users?locale=&seed=&batch=` | the same batch as JSON |
| `GET /api/benchmark?locale=&count=` | runs `fk_benchmark` |
| `GET /docs` | this document |
